articles.title: Pinning down the structure of quark-gluon plasma, the universe's first fluid
articles.dek: In the first fraction of a second following the Big Bang, matter existed as a trillion-degree plasma of quarks and gluons—subatomic particles that zinged around at close to…
paragraphs: In the first fraction of a second following the Big Bang, matter existed as a trillion-degree plasma of quarks and gluons—subatomic particles that zinged around at close to the speed of light. This roiling soup lasted for just a few microseconds before the particles coalesced into more stable protons and neutrons.

To study this primordial fluid, scientists recreate quark-gluon plasma in large particle accelerators, where ions are smashed together at close to the speed of light. These collisions create droplets of plasma roughly the size of an atomic nucleus that exist for only tens of septillionths of a second.

One way scientists study this plasma is by tracking other particles, such as heavy quarks, that are not part of the plasma but happen to move through it. The way a heavy particle moves through a fluid should tell something about the microscopic structure of the fluid itself. This general relationship was established famously by physicist Albert Einstein in 1905.

But in such extreme conditions, where particles are moving at close to the speed of light, something in Einstein's theory starts to break down; there are interactions within the plasma that the theory can't quite capture.

Now, physicists at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have taken up where Einstein's theory left off. They have worked out a theory that predicts how a relativistic particle, moving at close to the speed of light, is likely to be pushed and pulled by a fluid as it flies through it.

The researchers envision that the new theory could be applied to predict how a heavy quark will move through quark-gluon plasma. Such predictions could then be compared to experiments to characterize the microscopic structure of quark-gluon plasma and what kind of fluid must have existed in the universe's first moments.

"Our result reveals a new source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," says Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics—a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside."
Du Plessis and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB report their findings in Physical Review Letters .

In 1905, Einstein developed a theory to describe a particle's motion through fluid and how that motion can reveal the fluid's microscopic structure. His theory was inspired by the botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown observed a surprising phenomenon: Grains of pollen appeared to randomly jiggle and swirl when suspended in seemingly still water. This curious jittering of particles in fluid was later named "Brownian motion."

Einstein's 1905 theory showed that Brownian motion was a product of invisible, microscopic forces within the fluid. A particle's motion is a balance between the drag that the fluid exerts on the particle to slow it down and the random kicks within the fluid that keep the particle moving. These random kicks, Einstein argued, must come from microscopic forces within the fluid, exerted by none other than the atoms and molecules that make up the fluid. The energy of these microscopic particles can add up to kick and jostle larger particles.

Since he first published his theory, scientists have applied Einstein's explanation of Brownian motion to characterize a host of fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. As with most other fluids, it was assumed that a particle moving through quark-gluon plasma should experience a similar balance of microscopic kicks as a grain of pollen moving through water.

This balance is represented by a bell-shaped probability distribution, where a particle is most likely to experience medium-strength kicks (the highest point of the bell) and has an equally low probability of experiencing the most extreme kicks (the tail ends of the bell) as the particle moves through and eventually settles into a fluid.

articles.title: What AI can lose when it makes Holocaust writings easier to read
articles.dek: In an Amsterdam prison during the Nazi occupation, Sal Bramson drew his cell on pieces of cotton cloth.
paragraphs: In an Amsterdam prison during the Nazi occupation, Sal Bramson drew his cell on pieces of cotton cloth. He added handwritten explanations and sent these messages to his mother, concealed inside a shirt collar among the prison laundry. The cloth could travel because it passed as something ordinary. Its material was part of what made communication possible.

I study Holocaust writings that survive on fragile or improvised surfaces. In these objects, the words and the things carrying them remain intimately connected. Bramson's captions guide his mother's eye around his cell. His drawings give shape to the space he describes. The small, crowded textile carries both his account of confinement and evidence of his effort to reach her.
What happens to these relationships when an archival object becomes data?

AI and other computational tools can make historical collections easier to search, transcribe and translate. These are substantial gains. A person unable to decipher handwriting or read the original language may encounter a document that would otherwise remain inaccessible. Yet the process of making words available can also obscure the material evidence through which they survive.

My recent study , published in AI & Society , examines this problem through a concept I call "material uncertainty." It describes writing whose meaning remains bound to the damaged, improvised or unstable form in which it reaches us. The uncertainty may concern the circumstances of composition, the surface carrying the words, their intended recipient or the route by which the object entered an archive. These relationships shape what the writing allows us to know, including what remains unresolved.

I followed digital reproductions of three Holocaust writings through a sequence of computational operations: enhancing images, separating regions, recognizing handwriting, correcting and translating text, and generating descriptions for searchable records. I examined what each operation preserved or weakened. I used these deliberately difficult cases to trace how particular workflows change an object's representation. The study makes no claim to measure AI's overall accuracy.

Bramson's cloth showed how an apparently helpful operation could complicate interpretation. Suppressing the visible weave made some marks easier to distinguish. Separating drawings from writing helped organize the image for processing. But the textile was the means of concealment, and the captions and drawings worked together to address his mother. Handwriting recognition also produced fragments that correction could make plausible without establishing what Bramson had actually written.

A second object was an illustrated pencil poem by Eva Schulzová, a child imprisoned in Terezín. Her page moves between the camp's exterior, the women's bunks and an imagined meal of turkey and cake. The placement of words and drawings participates in that movement. She was later deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau, where she was murdered.

The workflow recovered much of her verbal text. Yet its generated description listed the illustrations without adequately representing their relationship to the poem. It described the imagined meal as a "food still life." I read that imagined abundance in relation to the child's confinement and hunger. The label gives little sense of that relationship. A searchable description can be informative and still leave the reader far from the work it describes.

Eliezer Heiman's paired clay tablets posed a different difficulty. Inscribed in Hebrew while he was in hiding in the Kovno ghetto, they record names and address future generations. Their paired form recalls the biblical Tablets of the Law. The surviving surface bears smoke staining and flaking, while the letters are cut into the clay.

In a photograph, shadows cast by engraved letters and damaged areas can look alike. The workflow could enhance some features but could not reliably separate inscription from deterioration. Here, the problem began with how the object was photographed. Imaging it under multiple lighting directions could better record its relief.

That distinction matters for anyone building an archive. Some evidence is missing because the initial image never captured it. Other evidence is visible in the image but becomes less accessible when processing separates elements that belong together. These problems require different responses.

articles.title: New research explores how offshore wind development may alter marine food webs
articles.dek: As offshore wind development expands along the U. S. Atlantic Coast, understanding its potential effects on marine ecosystems is increasingly important.
paragraphs: As offshore wind development expands along the U. S. Atlantic Coast, understanding its potential effects on marine ecosystems is increasingly important.

A newly published study in Scientific Reports , led by Kim Lato, a BRI scientist and postdoctoral research associate at the University of New Hampshire, examines how offshore wind infrastructure may alter seafloor communities, marine food webs and the movement of energy through marine ecosystems.

The study, "Assessing potential impacts of offshore wind development on U. S. marine ecosystems using food web modeling," is the first publication from BRI's Projecting the Effects of Offshore Wind-Mediated Benthic Changes on U. S. Marine Ecosystems project .

Offshore wind turbine foundations and associated structures introduce hard surfaces into marine environments that are often dominated by soft sediments. These structures can function as artificial reefs , creating habitat for organisms such as mussels, barnacles and other invertebrates. As these communities develop, they may alter how energy and nutrients move through the marine food web, potentially affecting fish and other marine species.

To investigate these changes, Lato and an international team of collaborators synthesized existing ecological data and developed food web models for three offshore wind development sites in the U. S. Atlantic. The models compared conditions before construction to observed (or projected) conditions approximately four years after construction, allowing researchers to explore potential changes in ecosystem structure, function and stability.
The results suggest that offshore wind development may contribute to shifts toward more mature and stable marine food webs, although responses varied across study sites and ecological measures.

The study identified sediment-dwelling invertebrates as particularly important to food web dynamics across the modeled scenarios. Among organisms associated with turbine structures, bivalves such as mussels emerged as especially influential, highlighting their potential role in altering energy flows and interactions among marine species.
Researchers also identified significant gaps in existing ecological data, particularly concerning microorganisms and the processes that recycle organic matter and nutrients within marine food webs.

These findings provide a foundation for identifying research priorities and improving environmental monitoring as offshore wind development continues along the Atlantic Coast. The research provides a framework for investigating how offshore wind infrastructure may influence marine ecosystems and informing future conservation and management decisions.

articles.title: Leaf nutrient balance helps explain earlier fall color in US forests
articles.dek: For devout leaf peepers, timing is everything. A new study led by researchers from Duke University's Nicholas School of the Environment shows that leaf nutrient levels affect…
paragraphs: For devout leaf peepers, timing is everything. A new study led by researchers from Duke University's Nicholas School of the Environment shows that leaf nutrient levels affect the onset of fall color. The findings, published in Nature Communications , could improve leaf drop forecasts and carbon cycle tracking.

Starting roughly in September in the United States, deciduous trees—species that seasonally drop their leaves—stop making the green pigment chlorophyll, used in photosynthesis. As other pigments become visible, leaves shift to shades of turmeric and crimson before dropping off. By mid-November, most deciduous trees are bare.

That process, called senescence, is a tree's way of conserving energy for winter. As days shorten, less sunlight is available to leaves to convert carbon dioxide from the air into life-sustaining sugars. Photosynthesis, which is energy-intensive, basically becomes more trouble than it's worth for several months.

Although trees in a given locale start changing color at roughly the same time each year, environmental factors such as temperature and rainfall can affect autumn leaf senescence. For example, more rain during autumn can extend how long leaves cling to trees.

Nutrients in leaves also play a role in senescence. For instance, the elements nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium regulate critical leaf processes, including chlorophyll production and the transport and use of sugars.

Those same nutrients are also important components of fertilizers used on crops. Their release into the environment could disrupt the balance of nutrients in leaves and therefore alter the timing of senescence, according to Tong Qiu, assistant professor of ecology at the Nicholas School, who oversaw the new study.

However, measuring nutrient levels in leaves has traditionally been labor-intensive and expensive, inhibiting evidence-based research on autumn senescence. "Usually, measuring nutrients requires people to collect leaves and go back to the lab and do an experiment to quantify their concentrations," Qiu says.

To work around those obstacles, Qiu and a multi-institutional team turned to the National Ecological Observatory Network, or NEON. NEON assembles troves of ecological data collected by remote-sensing instruments, such as satellites and airplanes, and by researchers in the field.

The data cover "a diverse range of ecosystems, from boreal tundra to tropical rainforest and dry forest, and to eastern deciduous forest and western conifers," says Hanshi Chen, a Ph. D. candidate at the Nicholas School and the study's first author.

The team first chose 25 U. S. forests representing different species compositions and locations. Using NEON, they assembled remote-sensing data on hundreds of different wavelengths of light reflected and absorbed by the forests. From that spectral data, they derived information about nutrient content in tree canopies.
Next, the researchers used statistical models to determine how ratios of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium affected senescence in each forest.

They found that higher ratios of nitrogen to phosphorus—that is, more nitrogen, less phosphorus—were associated with earlier senescence across 20 forests, regardless of climate, elevation, species composition and tree canopy structure. By contrast, canopies with a high ratio of nitrogen to potassium were slower to drop leaves.
"There seems to be a sweet spot where nitrogen and phosphorus are in balance. If that gets crossed, trees will start changing color earlier," Qiu says.
Further analysis indicated that higher ratios of nitrogen to phosphorus cause stress to leaves, likely causing them to shut down photosynthesis and drop sooner.

articles.title: New research explores what our appetite for a digital detox can tell us
articles.dek: How we feel about taking a break from our screens could tell us something important about the way we behave online, according to new research from the University of Bath and…
paragraphs: How we feel about taking a break from our screens could tell us something important about the way we behave online, according to new research from the University of Bath and Goethe University Frankfurt. Researchers have developed the first validated scale specifically designed to measure people's attitudes toward temporarily reducing their digital consumption, finding considerable differences in how positively people view the prospect of switching off.

The researchers say measuring these attitudes provides a new way to investigate our increasingly complex relationship with digital technology, including what makes people want to disconnect, why some are more receptive to the idea than others and whether that willingness ultimately translates into changes in behavior. More than eight in 10 participants were positive about the idea of a digital detox, suggesting a widespread appetite for switching off, although the study did not test whether they subsequently did so.

Published in Psychology & Marketing , the research found that attitudes toward digital detox were associated with characteristics including mindfulness and self-control. They could also help predict how much time people subsequently spent watching online videos.

From work emails and instant messaging to social media, push notifications and AI-driven recommendations, digital technology increasingly competes for our attention. Digital detox, deliberately reducing our use of digital devices for a period of time, has emerged as one response to this constant connectivity.

Goethe University Frankfurt professor Jan Landwehr said, "Many people feel overwhelmed by the constant digital information flow and experience a need to switch off. We developed a scientifically validated measurement scale to make this vague positive attitude toward reducing digital activities measurable. And we find that a vast majority of our participants have a latent need to detox from digital activities."

The team developed the Attitude toward Digital Detox (ADD) scale, a seven-item measure of how positively people feel about temporarily reducing their digital consumption. Across seven studies, the researchers tested the scale with a mix of participants, including adult U. S. residents recruited through online research platforms, university students in Central Europe, members of Reddit communities focused on online and offline activities and consumer-behavior experts from European universities.

Goethe University Frankfurt professor Torsten Bornemann said: "The scale could now be used to explore when and why people want to reduce their digital consumption and whether changing attitudes toward switching off might ultimately help people take greater control of their relationship with technology."

articles.title: Plastic bags and bottles become industrial-strength adhesives through new upcycling method
articles.dek: Around 450 million metric tons of plastics are produced worldwide each year.
paragraphs: Around 450 million metric tons of plastics are produced worldwide each year. The major share of this sheer volume is used only once and then winds up in an incinerator or in landfills. This also applies to so-called polyolefins, which include polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP). As packaging materials and films, they account for approximately half of our plastic consumption.

Although polyolefins can be melted down and recast into new shapes, this process results in significant quality losses. The dyes in the waste impart a dark color to the recycled material, while the heating process damages its quality: as a result, the material is only suitable for low-grade applications such as plant pots or paving slabs.
So far, it has proved impossible to selectively break down polyolefins into their basic building blocks—the monomers—from which new, high-quality polymers could be synthesized.

Olefins, which consist exclusively of carbon and hydrogen, lack the oxygen, nitrogen or chlorine atoms required for targeted cleavage reactions. To date, the only feasible method is random breakdown by way of an energy-intensive heating process known as pyrolysis . This produces petroleum-based feedstocks from which the monomers must be rebuilt.

Now, a team of researchers led by polymer chemist and ETH Professor Tae-Lim Choi has developed a process that allows polyolefins to be upcycled into higher-value plastics, rather than simply being recycled in a manner that reduces their value. To achieve this, they graft additional polymer chains with new functionalities onto the plastics.
The research is published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society . ETH Zurich has patented the process and nominated it for the Spark Award.

Hongsik Kim, the senior scientist in Choi's group who was primarily responsible for developing the method, produced adhesives as the first product using standard plastic bags and bottles. Their adhesive strength with various materials such as metal, glass or wood meets the requirements for an industrial adhesive employed in load-bearing and high-stress joints in vehicle or equipment manufacturing.

The range of potential applications, however, is much broader: the additional polymer chains allow the entire spectrum of chemical functionalities to be introduced into polyolefins: from polar groups that interact with water to varying degrees, through acids and bases, to chemical groups capable of undergoing very specific reactions.

Chlorinated solvents are a key chemical component of the process. When irradiated with short-wavelength light, these solvents can generate highly reactive individual chlorine atoms, known as radicals. These transfer their reactivity to carbon atoms in the polyolefin chains, resulting in carbon radicals, which can be used as a starting point for the synthesis of additional polymer chains.

The idea of using chlorinated solvents to create reactive sites in the polyolefin chains stems from a collaboration between Choi and the group led by Athina Anastasaki, Professor of Sustainable Polymers at ETH Zurich. She has applied this principle to the recycling of acrylic glass, also known under the brand name Plexiglas.

The major advantages of the newly patented method are the fact that it is extremely simple, does not require expensive special reagents or catalysts, and does not necessitate high process temperatures.
The entire process takes place in a single step: the plastic waste is dissolved in a chlorinated solvent, after which the monomers required for the synthesis of the desired graft polymer are added.

Furthermore, the process can be precisely controlled. "We are able to control how many radicals are generated—and consequently how many sites in the polyolefin chains are activated for grafting—by adjusting the degree of chlorination of the solvent and the wavelength of the light as required," explains Kim.

articles.title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting block than some other Democratic candidates
articles.dek: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U. S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections.
paragraphs: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U. S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections.

As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals , as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.

The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U. S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black .

After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide.

About 91. 8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results . Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms , up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.
In fact, El-Sayed received 70. 6% of Wayne County votes , which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62. 7% of the vote in Wayne County .
In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48. 3% , from 50. 6% in 2020 , as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris.

Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48. 6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote.

In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.

Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.

Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024.

While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide , Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll .

Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed . NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson , who won the governorship over Republican John James.
Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement.
Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate .

However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity . Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates.

Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination . If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.
My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations.

El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program , while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education.

El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience . El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries.

Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U. S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U. S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U. S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election . Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day.
“I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.

articles.title: Less Sugar in Early Life Could Protect Your Mental Health Decades Later
articles.dek: An observational study links sugar rationing in early life to lower adult anxiety and depression risks, raising the possibility that our earliest diets have lasting mental…
paragraphs: An observational study links sugar rationing in early life to lower adult anxiety and depression risks, raising the possibility that our earliest diets have lasting mental health implications.

Could the amount of sugar we consume before birth and during infancy influence our mental health decades later? An experiment rooted in postwar Britain suggests that the effects of our earliest diets may extend far beyond childhood.

During World War II and the years that followed, the United Kingdom strictly rationed sugar, limiting how much families could purchase. When those restrictions ended in September 1953, sugar consumption surged, creating a rare opportunity for scientists to examine how early-life exposure to sugar might shape long-term health.

A study published in General Psychiatry found that exposure to rationing during early life was associated with a 17% lower risk of anxiety and a 14% lower risk of depression compared with no exposure. The researchers analyzed data from 66,223 UK Biobank participants born around the policy change, linking the timing of their earliest years to health records later in life.

Because the availability of other foods remained relatively stable when sugar consumption increased, the end of rationing offered a natural experiment. Researchers could compare people who experienced different periods of restricted sugar availability at the start of life. They estimated exposure using birth dates relative to the policy change, with exposure ranging from before birth only to periods extending through about age two.

That approach tracked exposure to a national policy, rather than measuring what individual mothers or children ate. The researchers did not have individual childhood food records, and unmeasured factors, including other aspects of maternal diet, may have influenced the results. The findings therefore cannot establish that lower sugar intake caused the differences in mental health.

The strongest associations appeared among people exposed to rationing throughout the first 1,000 days after conception, spanning pregnancy and roughly the first two years after birth. Compared with people without early exposure, this group had approximately 24% lower relative risk of anxiety and 21% lower relative risk of depression. Across the analysis, the association generally strengthened with longer exposure to rationing.

For participants exposed throughout those first 1,000 days, diagnoses also appeared later in their health records. The first recorded anxiety diagnosis occurred about two years later, and the first recorded depression diagnosis about four years later, than among participants with no early exposure. These findings concern when diagnoses were first recorded, rather than necessarily when symptoms began.

Early nutrition could potentially influence later mental health through its effects on stress regulation, inflammation, and brain development. The authors drew these possible explanations from previous research, but did not directly test the mechanisms in the UK Biobank analysis. Further studies that measure individual diets and examine other populations will help clarify how dietary conditions during pregnancy and infancy relate to mental health across the life course, and what that relationship could mean for public health.

articles.title: Animal vs. Plant Protein: New Study Reveals Unexpected Testosterone Differences
articles.dek: An observational study of middle-aged men links animal protein to lower testosterone and plant protein to higher levels, but the differences are small, and their health…
paragraphs: An observational study of middle-aged men links animal protein to lower testosterone and plant protein to higher levels, but the differences are small, and their health effects remain unclear.

A protein-rich meal gives the body amino acids, the building blocks it needs to make and repair tissues, including muscle. Testosterone helps regulate muscle growth and also supports bones and sexual function. Food provides essential materials, while hormones help direct what the body does with them.
That connection makes diet a reasonable place to look when studying testosterone, yet relatively few studies have examined its relationship with protein intake.

Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland found that men who consumed more animal protein tended to have lower total testosterone levels in their blood. Those who consumed more plant protein tended to have higher levels. The findings do not mean that higher testosterone is necessarily healthier or that one protein source improves hormone function.

The research, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition , included 2,546 men aged 42 to 60 living in eastern Finland. It drew on the university’s ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study. Researchers assessed the men’s diets using four-day food records collected between 1984 and 1989 and measured total testosterone in blood samples. They also measured sex hormone-binding globulin, or SHBG, a protein that binds to sex hormones and influences total testosterone concentrations in the blood.

Looking at individual foods revealed a distinction that the broad category of animal protein could obscure. Higher dairy protein intake was associated with lower total testosterone and SHBG levels. Meat protein intake was associated with lower SHBG, but it had no association with total testosterone. Among plant foods, higher protein intake from vegetables and sources other than cereal products was associated with higher total testosterone.

To compare the differences, the researchers divided the men into four groups according to their protein intake. Those in the highest animal protein group had total testosterone concentrations averaging 1. 2 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L) below those in the lowest group. For plant protein, the highest intake group averaged 1. 1 nmol/L above the lowest group. SHBG showed similar opposing associations with animal and plant protein intake.

“Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health,” says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

Age, excess weight, and lifestyle can influence testosterone levels. The analyses accounted for the men’s age and body mass index, along with several other dietary, lifestyle, and health factors. Even with those adjustments, other aspects of their diets or metabolic factors could help explain the associations.

Because the study was cross-sectional, it cannot establish that eating particular proteins caused the hormone differences. It also cannot determine whether consuming different protein sources affects how much testosterone the body produces or how the hormone acts in the body.

articles.title: Scientists Unlock a Hidden Superconducting Power Inside a Strange Quantum Material
articles.dek: Researchers have discovered how pressure can unlock hidden superconducting properties in a complex quantum material.
paragraphs: Researchers have discovered how pressure can unlock hidden superconducting properties in a complex quantum material.

Applying intense pressure to an unusual quantum material can transform how it conducts electricity, allowing superconductivity to spread throughout its three-dimensional structure at temperatures roughly three times higher than normal. Researchers also found a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity.

The discovery comes from a team led by Zurab Guguchia at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland. Their findings, published in Nature Communications , provide new insight into how superconductivity might be strengthened and eventually achieved under more practical conditions.
Tantalum disulfide has a simple chemical composition but a remarkably complex electronic structure. It consists of extremely thin atomic layers that behave differently as temperatures fall.
“Its chemical formula sounds very simple: for every tantalum atom there are two sulfur atoms,” says Guguchia. “But inside it is an enormously complex material with almost paradoxical properties.”

When produced in a particular way, the material contains alternating layers with two distinct atomic arrangements. Both conduct electricity at higher temperatures, but cooling causes one to become an insulator while the other becomes superconducting, carrying current without electrical resistance. “This means that the electronic properties of these two layers behave in completely opposite ways,” Guguchia explains.

Initially, superconductivity remains confined to individual conducting layers because the insulating layers obstruct electron movement between them. But cooling the material to just over 1 kelvin (about −458°F) produces a dramatic change.

“Suddenly the entire material becomes superconducting, so the insulating layers also become conductive and take part in superconductivity,” Guguchia says. Instead of remaining restricted to separate planes, superconductivity extends throughout the crystal in three dimensions.

Scientists knew that applying pressure could raise the temperature at which this transition occurs, but the underlying mechanisms were unclear. The PSI team investigated how compression affects the material’s electrons and the interactions between its layers.

The researchers subjected tantalum disulfide to pressures several hundred times greater than those inside a typical car tire. Compression brought the superconducting layers closer together, reducing the disruptive effect of the insulating layers. It also allowed previously localized electrons within the insulating layers to participate in superconductivity.

“Due to these effects, high pressure causes tantalum disulfide to become superconducting in all three dimensions at temperatures approximately three times higher.” Measurements also revealed a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity.

“So, pressure not only raises the temperature at which superconductivity can occur, but also changes the very nature of the superconducting state,” the researcher explained. “It alters the way electrons pair up and move together through the material, resulting in a more robust form of superconductivity.”

To investigate these changes, the team used muon spin spectroscopy, a technique that detects magnetic conditions inside materials. Muons are elementary particles similar to electrons but approximately 200 times heavier. Although they survive for only a few millionths of a second, their sensitivity to local magnetic fields makes them especially useful for studying superconductors.
“Since muons are exceptionally sensitive probes for magnetic and superconducting properties, we can gain unique insights into quantum materials here at PSI,” Guguchia says.

articles.title: A Hidden Star May Be Plowing Through Betelgeuse’s Giant Atmosphere
articles.dek: Radio images suggest a link between Betelgeuse’s changing outline and its companion’s expected orbit, offering clues to how a smaller star may influence a giant’s later life.
paragraphs: Radio images suggest a link between Betelgeuse’s changing outline and its companion’s expected orbit, offering clues to how a smaller star may influence a giant’s later life.

Betelgeuse, the bright red supergiant marking Orion’s shoulder, may have another star stirring its atmosphere from within. Its recently identified companion, Siwarha, is thought to orbit at a distance of only about twice the giant’s radius. New radio observations suggest that this close neighbor is leaving a visible mark on the shape of Betelgeuse’s outer gas, even though the companion itself is too faint to appear in those observations.

Researchers proposed Siwarha’s existence in 2024 to explain Betelgeuse’s mysterious 2,100-day brightness cycle. Direct imaging and spectroscopic studies of the star’s light have since supported its existence. The companion’s name means “her bracelet,” a reference to Betelgeuse’s Arabic meaning, “the hand of al-Jawza.”

The new study was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, with colleagues from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team combined observations from the U. S. National Science Foundation’s Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), collected between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 to 485 GHz.

Radio waves at different frequencies reveal different depths in a star’s atmosphere. Using both observatories allowed the researchers to build a picture of Betelgeuse layer by layer, from just above its visible surface to several times the star’s radius.

“It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here,” said Matthews. “The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing.”

Detecting Siwarha directly was beyond the observations’ reach. The team calculated that the companion would be tens to hundreds of times too faint to see at radio wavelengths. They could, however, measure the ellipticity of Betelgeuse’s radio-emitting atmosphere, meaning how stretched or egg-shaped it appeared, at different observing times.

The atmosphere looked noticeably more elongated near the times when Siwarha was expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from Betelgeuse. It appeared rounder when the companion was expected to pass in front of or behind the giant star. That correspondence suggests that the smaller star’s gravity and movement are disturbing the surrounding gas.

“This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere,” Matthews explained. Its passage could leave a wake, much as a boat leaves one as it moves through water.
The team will need observations covering more of Siwarha’s orbit, particularly at frequencies that have not yet been well sampled, to confirm and refine these findings.

The same radio data also show that Betelgeuse’s extended atmosphere has largely recovered from a much more conspicuous disturbance. In late 2019 and early 2020, the star faded to its faintest level in more than a century of record-keeping. During that episode, known as the Great Dimming, Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of stellar material that partially blocked our view.

Months before the dimming, a 2019 study led by Matthews had found that Betelgeuse’s atmosphere was unusually cool at radio wavelengths. That team proposed that convection, the circulation of gas carrying heat from deep within the star, had triggered a shock wave. The wave could have disturbed gas in the outer layers, setting the stage for the massive dust-forming outburst that followed.

The new measurements show that the atmosphere’s brightness temperature, a temperature inferred from the strength of its radio emission, has returned to more typical levels at those same wavelengths. At a distance from the center of about 2. 7 times Betelgeuse’s radius, the gas now registers around 3,500 kelvin, or about 5,840°F. That is comparable to the temperature of the star’s visible surface.

Closer to the surface, the highest-frequency ALMA measurements revealed a much cooler layer. These observations probed nearer to Betelgeuse’s surface than previous radio measurements and found temperatures of roughly 2,200 kelvin, or about 3,500°F. That is more than 1,000 kelvin cooler than the photosphere, the star’s visible surface.

articles.title: NASA Astronauts to Answer Questions from Florida Students
articles.dek: Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station .
paragraphs: Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station .
The Earth-to-space call will begin at 10:40 a. m. EST Tuesday, Nov. 10, and will stream live on the agency’s Learn With NASA YouTube channel.

This event is hosted by Freedom Crossing Academy in St. Johns, Florida, for students in grades K-12, and the community. This unique opportunity aims to deepen understanding of space exploration and enhance awareness of STEM careers.
Media interested in covering the event must RSVP no later than 5 p. m. EST, Monday, Nov. 9, to Christina Upchurch at (904) 547-7517, or at christina. upchurch@stjohns. k12. fl. us .

For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth. The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis program, and to Mars.

articles.title: A Black Hole Could Split in Two, According to a Surprising New Theory
articles.dek: Black holes might split in two under extreme conditions, theoretical calculations suggest, offering physicists a way to explore the limits of our understanding of gravity.
paragraphs: Black holes might split in two under extreme conditions, theoretical calculations suggest, offering physicists a way to explore the limits of our understanding of gravity.

Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could a single black hole divide into two smaller ones that go their separate ways? Reversing a merger might sound straightforward, but the rules governing black holes make it difficult.

One obstacle is entropy, a measure of how many different microscopic arrangements can give a physical system the same overall properties. Think of rolling two dice. Several combinations produce a total of seven, but only two ones produce a total of two. Entropy captures a similar distinction between an overall result and the different underlying arrangements that can produce it. More possible arrangements mean higher entropy.

For an ordinary black hole that is not rotating, two smaller black holes would have less combined entropy than the original. That makes splitting thermodynamically unfavorable. The usual requirement of thermodynamics is that the total entropy of an isolated system should stay the same or increase, rather than decrease.

Whether black holes can split is the subject of “When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies,” a theoretical study published in Physical Review D . The unusual title describes what a split would look like through time. A black hole’s outer boundary, called its horizon, would trace a trouser-like shape, with one section dividing into two “legs.”

“In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen”, says Francesco Sannino, a co-author and professor of physics at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.

Sannino’s co-authors are Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) researcher at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint laboratory of CNRS and Sorbonne Université in Paris, and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.

Their calculations suggest that rapid rotation could offer a loophole in the thermodynamic barrier. A spinning black hole might be able to divide under conditions that would make splitting unfavorable for a nonrotating one.

“But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate,” says Francesco Sannino.

The researchers also explore theories with additional dimensions of space. Within these theories, physicists already know of black-hole-like objects that can become unstable and begin to break apart. Under some of these conditions, splitting can be thermodynamically favorable, particularly when one resulting black hole is much smaller than the other. Even then, showing that entropy permits a split does not establish that the process will actually happen.
The possibilities also extend to primordial black holes, hypothetical objects that could have formed in the early universe.

“We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein’s theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers,” says Francesco Sannino.
